chunks: "A chiplet is a small die designed to be one piece of a bigger system.
Instead of building one huge monolithic chip, you build several smaller dies, test them, and then assemble the good ones into a single package, and the package behaves like one chip.
The main reason is yield. Defects land randomly on a wafer, so a big die is much more likely to contain one than a small die.
If I split an 800 mm² design into four 200 mm² chiplets and only keep the good ones, I throw away far less silicon.
The second reason is flexibility: the compute dies can use the newest, most expensive process, while I/O and analog, which don't shrink well, stay on an older cheaper node.
Third, you can reuse one chiplet across many products, like AMD does with its CPU chiplets and a separate I/O die. The costs are real though.

The links between chiplets are longer than on-die wires, so you pay latency and energy per bit, you need advanced packaging with fine-pitch bumps or an interposer, and you have to test known good dies up front.
Heat also concentrates because many hot dies sit close together. So it's a trade of silicon cost against packaging complexity."
